MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

DUALChina's state megaconstellation, catalogued under the literal Chinese hulianwang digui (internet, low orbit) rather than its programme name. Run by China SatNet (中国星网), a central SOE created in 2021 and reporting to SASAC, not to CASC. Two ITU-filed shells: GW-A59, 6,080 satellites at 500–600 km, and GW-2, 6,912 at ~1,145 km — 12,992 in all. Deployment is batched by rocket: Long March 5B carries 10 per flight, Long March 8A and Long March 12 nine, Long March 6A five from Taiyuan. The 2026 groups have gone to two inclinations, ~50° and ~86.5°, though published tracking does not map groups to shells cleanly. Stated ramp is 310 satellites in 2026, 900 in 2027 and 3,600 a year from 2028; the counted cadence is running behind that. No broadband service had opened to subscribers as of October 2026 — the system is still in test. Military relevance is structural rather than declared: a sovereign, state-owned broadband layer is resilient communications infrastructure whoever the subscribers turn out to be.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

DUALChina's state megaconstellation, catalogued under the literal Chinese hulianwang digui (internet, low orbit) rather than its programme name. Run by China SatNet (中国星网), a central SOE created in 2021 and reporting to SASAC, not to CASC. Two ITU-filed shells: GW-A59, 6,080 satellites at 500–600 km, and GW-2, 6,912 at ~1,145 km — 12,992 in all. Deployment is batched by rocket: Long March 5B carries 10 per flight, Long March 8A and Long March 12 nine, Long March 6A five from Taiyuan. The 2026 groups have gone to two inclinations, ~50° and ~86.5°, though published tracking does not map groups to shells cleanly. Stated ramp is 310 satellites in 2026, 900 in 2027 and 3,600 a year from 2028; the counted cadence is running behind that. No broadband service had opened to subscribers as of October 2026 — the system is still in test. Military relevance is structural rather than declared: a sovereign, state-owned broadband layer is resilient communications infrastructure whoever the subscribers turn out to be.

COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. Filed for ~15,000 satellites; the flat-panel stackable bus is built on a production line explicitly modelled on Starlink's. Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

MILTongxin Jishu Shiyan (通信技术试验卫星, 'communications technology experiment satellite') — a cover designation, not a mission description. CASC announces each one with near-identical boilerplate about communications, broadcasting and data-transmission technology verification, and releases nothing further. The analyst consensus, led by Jonathan McDowell's GCAT and Gunter's Space Page, is that TJS bundles at least three distinct programmes: a Qianshao-3 SIGINT class, a Huoyan-1 missile early-warning class, and an unclassified remainder. Attribution to a class is inferred from orbit, launch vehicle and cadence, never confirmed — Gunter's notes that satellites grouped together on those grounds may turn out to have different missions.

COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. Filed for ~15,000 satellites; the flat-panel stackable bus is built on a production line explicitly modelled on Starlink's. Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

DUALHaiyang (海洋, 'ocean') — ocean colour, sea-surface temperature, salinity and sea-state satellites. The HY-2 series carries radar altimeters and microwave scatterometers; altimetry over the ocean is a civil oceanography product and a submarine- and surface-operations input at once.

MILTongxin Jishu Shiyan (通信技术试验卫星, 'communications technology experiment satellite') — a cover designation, not a mission description. CASC announces each one with near-identical boilerplate about communications, broadcasting and data-transmission technology verification, and releases nothing further. The analyst consensus, led by Jonathan McDowell's GCAT and Gunter's Space Page, is that TJS bundles at least three distinct programmes: a Qianshao-3 SIGINT class, a Huoyan-1 missile early-warning class, and an unclassified remainder. Attribution to a class is inferred from orbit, launch vehicle and cadence, never confirmed — Gunter's notes that satellites grouped together on those grounds may turn out to have different missions.

DUALChina's state megaconstellation, catalogued under the literal Chinese hulianwang digui (internet, low orbit) rather than its programme name. Run by China SatNet (中国星网), a central SOE created in 2021 and reporting to SASAC, not to CASC. Two ITU-filed shells: GW-A59, 6,080 satellites at 500–600 km, and GW-2, 6,912 at ~1,145 km — 12,992 in all. Deployment is batched by rocket: Long March 5B carries 10 per flight, Long March 8A and Long March 12 nine, Long March 6A five from Taiyuan. The 2026 groups have gone to two inclinations, ~50° and ~86.5°, though published tracking does not map groups to shells cleanly. Stated ramp is 310 satellites in 2026, 900 in 2027 and 3,600 a year from 2028; the counted cadence is running behind that. No broadband service had opened to subscribers as of October 2026 — the system is still in test. Military relevance is structural rather than declared: a sovereign, state-owned broadband layer is resilient communications infrastructure whoever the subscribers turn out to be.

DUALShijian (实践, 'practice') is China's long-running technology-demonstration line, and the label covers everything from benign materials experiments to the most closely watched spacecraft in the catalogue. Several Shijian vehicles have performed documented rendezvous and proximity operations in GEO; commercial trackers (ExoAnalytic, COMSPOC) and ISR University follow them because an inspection capability and a co-orbital counterspace capability are the same hardware pointed at different targets.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

MILTongxin Jishu Shiyan (通信技术试验卫星, 'communications technology experiment satellite') — a cover designation, not a mission description. CASC announces each one with near-identical boilerplate about communications, broadcasting and data-transmission technology verification, and releases nothing further. The analyst consensus, led by Jonathan McDowell's GCAT and Gunter's Space Page, is that TJS bundles at least three distinct programmes: a Qianshao-3 SIGINT class, a Huoyan-1 missile early-warning class, and an unclassified remainder. Attribution to a class is inferred from orbit, launch vehicle and cadence, never confirmed — Gunter's notes that satellites grouped together on those grounds may turn out to have different missions.
CIVShenzhou (神舟, 'divine vessel') — China's crewed spacecraft, now flying rotation missions to the Tiangong station.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

COMJilin-1, operated by Chang Guang Satellite Technology — a spin-out of the CAS Changchun Institute and China's largest commercial imaging constellation, with video as well as still capability. Chang Guang has stated a 300-satellite goal. Commercially sold imagery with a declared revisit rate fine enough to be operationally useful, which is why the constellation appears in military-utility assessments despite its private ownership.

DUALChina's state megaconstellation, catalogued under the literal Chinese hulianwang digui (internet, low orbit) rather than its programme name. Run by China SatNet (中国星网), a central SOE created in 2021 and reporting to SASAC, not to CASC. Two ITU-filed shells: GW-A59, 6,080 satellites at 500–600 km, and GW-2, 6,912 at ~1,145 km — 12,992 in all. Deployment is batched by rocket: Long March 5B carries 10 per flight, Long March 8A and Long March 12 nine, Long March 6A five from Taiyuan. The 2026 groups have gone to two inclinations, ~50° and ~86.5°, though published tracking does not map groups to shells cleanly. Stated ramp is 310 satellites in 2026, 900 in 2027 and 3,600 a year from 2028; the counted cadence is running behind that. No broadband service had opened to subscribers as of October 2026 — the system is still in test. Military relevance is structural rather than declared: a sovereign, state-owned broadband layer is resilient communications infrastructure whoever the subscribers turn out to be.

Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

MILBroke up in orbit in September 2026. CelesTrak published no fragment element sets for the event, and the debris appears in NAZAR's Debris Tracker only through the Space-Track catalogue.

DUALChina's state megaconstellation, catalogued under the literal Chinese hulianwang digui (internet, low orbit) rather than its programme name. Run by China SatNet (中国星网), a central SOE created in 2021 and reporting to SASAC, not to CASC. Two ITU-filed shells: GW-A59, 6,080 satellites at 500–600 km, and GW-2, 6,912 at ~1,145 km — 12,992 in all. Deployment is batched by rocket: Long March 5B carries 10 per flight, Long March 8A and Long March 12 nine, Long March 6A five from Taiyuan. The 2026 groups have gone to two inclinations, ~50° and ~86.5°, though published tracking does not map groups to shells cleanly. Stated ramp is 310 satellites in 2026, 900 in 2027 and 3,600 a year from 2028; the counted cadence is running behind that. No broadband service had opened to subscribers as of October 2026 — the system is still in test. Military relevance is structural rather than declared: a sovereign, state-owned broadband layer is resilient communications infrastructure whoever the subscribers turn out to be.

Stated ramp is 310 satellites in 2026, 900 in 2027 and 3,600 a year from 2028; the counted cadence is running behind that. No broadband service had opened to subscribers as of October 2026 — the system is still in test. Military relevance is structural rather than declared: a sovereign, state-owned broadband layer is resilient communications infrastructure whoever the subscribers turn out to be.

MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

DUALShijian (实践, 'practice') is China's long-running technology-demonstration line, and the label covers everything from benign materials experiments to the most closely watched spacecraft in the catalogue. Several Shijian vehicles have performed documented rendezvous and proximity operations in GEO; commercial trackers (ExoAnalytic, COMSPOC) and ISR University follow them because an inspection capability and a co-orbital counterspace capability are the same hardware pointed at different targets.

CIVFengyun (风云, 'wind and cloud') — China's operational meteorological satellites, in two families: odd numbers in sun-synchronous polar orbit, even numbers in geostationary. Fengyun data is distributed internationally through the WMO and is a genuine public good. The series also carries the programme's worst moment: the destruction of Fengyun-1C in the January 2007 ASAT test.

DUALShijian (实践, 'practice') is China's long-running technology-demonstration line, and the label covers everything from benign materials experiments to the most closely watched spacecraft in the catalogue. Several Shijian vehicles have performed documented rendezvous and proximity operations in GEO; commercial trackers (ExoAnalytic, COMSPOC) and ISR University follow them because an inspection capability and a co-orbital counterspace capability are the same hardware pointed at different targets.

MIL21 November 2025, Long March 3B from Xichang. CASC gave the standard communications-test boilerplate, but the launch went to a high inclination and SpaceNews reported it as heading for a Molniya-type orbit rather than the geostationary belt the series normally occupies. A Molniya orbit buys long dwell over high latitudes — the regime used for northern early warning and for communications above the GEO horizon.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. Filed for ~15,000 satellites; the flat-panel stackable bus is built on a production line explicitly modelled on Starlink's. Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

CIVFengyun (风云, 'wind and cloud') — China's operational meteorological satellites, in two families: odd numbers in sun-synchronous polar orbit, even numbers in geostationary. Fengyun data is distributed internationally through the WMO and is a genuine public good. The series also carries the programme's worst moment: the destruction of Fengyun-1C in the January 2007 ASAT test.
No public technical detail has been released for this satellite, and no series attribution is established in the open sources. Orbit, launch date and the COSPAR launch id are the available evidence.

MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

Two ITU-filed shells: GW-A59, 6,080 satellites at 500–600 km, and GW-2, 6,912 at ~1,145 km — 12,992 in all. Deployment is batched by rocket: Long March 5B carries 10 per flight, Long March 8A and Long March 12 nine, Long March 6A five from Taiyuan. The 2026 groups have gone to two inclinations, ~50° and ~86.5°, though published tracking does not map groups to shells cleanly. Stated ramp is 310 satellites in 2026, 900 in 2027 and 3,600 a year from 2028; the counted cadence is running behind that. No broadband service had opened to subscribers as of October 2026 — the system is still in test. Military relevance is structural rather than declared: a sovereign, state-owned broadband layer is resilient communications infrastructure whoever the subscribers turn out to be.

DUALShijian (实践, 'practice') is China's long-running technology-demonstration line, and the label covers everything from benign materials experiments to the most closely watched spacecraft in the catalogue. Several Shijian vehicles have performed documented rendezvous and proximity operations in GEO; commercial trackers (ExoAnalytic, COMSPOC) and ISR University follow them because an inspection capability and a co-orbital counterspace capability are the same hardware pointed at different targets.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

MILTianping (天平, 'balance') — radar calibration targets. Spheres and simple bodies of precisely known radar cross-section, used to calibrate ground radars and refine atmospheric-drag models. Unglamorous and quietly important: the accuracy of a space surveillance network is set by what it has to calibrate against.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. Filed for ~15,000 satellites; the flat-panel stackable bus is built on a production line explicitly modelled on Starlink's. Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. Filed for ~15,000 satellites; the flat-panel stackable bus is built on a production line explicitly modelled on Starlink's. Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

MILLaunched 23 January and stationed at 18.4°E — a slot over Africa, well west of China. McDowell's 2026 survey records it as possibly a Huoyan early-warning satellite; a westward slot suits watching launch areas that are not on China's own doorstep.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

DUALShijian-25, launched January 2025 to demonstrate on-orbit refuelling and life extension. Through 2025 it was observed closing on Shijian-21 in GEO in a long, carefully staged approach — the first Chinese satellite-servicing rendezvous between two of its own spacecraft, and watched by Western trackers for exactly the dual-use reason that refuelling hardware and grappling hardware are the same hardware.
MILCLASSMissile EW. 8th TJS in ~18 months.

DUALChina's state megaconstellation, catalogued under the literal Chinese hulianwang digui (internet, low orbit) rather than its programme name. Run by China SatNet (中国星网), a central SOE created in 2021 and reporting to SASAC, not to CASC. The 2026 groups have gone to two inclinations, ~50° and ~86.5°, though published tracking does not map groups to shells cleanly. COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

MILTianping (天平, 'balance') — radar calibration targets. Spheres and simple bodies of precisely known radar cross-section, used to calibrate ground radars and refine atmospheric-drag models. Unglamorous and quietly important: the accuracy of a space surveillance network is set by what it has to calibrate against.

DUALGaofen (高分, 'high resolution') is the space segment of CHEOS, the China High-resolution Earth Observation System, managed by SASTIND. The series splits cleanly at number 8: Gaofen-1 to -7 are genuinely civil, documented in eoPortal and WMO OSCAR with published instruments and open data, serving agriculture, disaster response and mapping. Gaofen-8 and above have had no technical detail released at all, which is itself the evidence analysts rely on — SpaceNews notes the information blackout above GF-7, and the USCC's counterspace assessment describes PRC space assets as assigned military or dual-use and mobilisable in a crisis. The civil branding is real; so is the military customer behind the higher numbers.

DUALHulianwan gaogui — internet, high orbit, against the digui (low orbit) of the main batches. These are the prototypes for Guowang's upper shell, the ~1,145 km GW-2 layer, where a smaller number of satellites covers the same ground at the cost of latency.

DUALShijian (实践, 'practice') is China's long-running technology-demonstration line, and the label covers everything from benign materials experiments to the most closely watched spacecraft in the catalogue. Several Shijian vehicles have performed documented rendezvous and proximity operations in GEO; commercial trackers (ExoAnalytic, COMSPOC) and ISR University follow them because an inspection capability and a co-orbital counterspace capability are the same hardware pointed at different targets.

DUALBeiDou is China's global navigation system and the strategic point of the whole programme: ending dependence on GPS, a system the US can degrade regionally at will. BDS-3 was declared complete in July 2020 with a 30-satellite core — 24 in MEO at ~21,500 km, 3 in inclined geosynchronous orbit (IGSO) and 3 in GEO. The IGSO and GEO components are what distinguish BeiDou's architecture from GPS: they concentrate signal strength and availability over China and the Asia-Pacific, including in urban canyons and at high latitudes where a pure MEO constellation thins out. BeiDou also carries a short-message two-way service GPS has no equivalent of. Earlier BDS-2 spacecraft remain in the catalogue, some operational, some drifting as spares or retired; replenishment BDS-3 launches have continued past the 2020 completion date, so the catalogue count runs well above the 30-satellite nominal constellation.

MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

COMThousand Sails (千帆), the Shanghai-backed commercial answer to Starlink, run by Spacesail (Shanghai Yuanxin Satellite Technology) out of the G60 science-and-technology corridor and funded substantially by the Shanghai municipal government. Filed for ~15,000 satellites; the flat-panel stackable bus is built on a production line explicitly modelled on Starlink's. Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

Distinct from Guowang in ownership and intent — Spacesail has signed overseas distribution agreements (Brazil, Kazakhstan, Malaysia among them), which makes it the outward-facing half of China's LEO broadband push. The satellites are notably bright, and the constellation has drawn the same astronomical objections as its Western analogue.

DUALGaofen (高分, 'high resolution') is the space segment of CHEOS, the China High-resolution Earth Observation System, managed by SASTIND. The series splits cleanly at number 8: Gaofen-1 to -7 are genuinely civil, documented in eoPortal and WMO OSCAR with published instruments and open data, serving agriculture, disaster response and mapping. Gaofen-8 and above have had no technical detail released at all, which is itself the evidence analysts rely on — SpaceNews notes the information blackout above GF-7, and the USCC's counterspace assessment describes PRC space assets as assigned military or dual-use and mobilisable in a crisis. The civil branding is real; so is the military customer behind the higher numbers.

UNKCatalogued by the US Space Force without a name being released or identified. Objects sit in this state for two quite different reasons: they are recent deployments from a megaconstellation batch that the catalogue has not yet matched to its programme designation, or they are payloads whose operator has never announced them. Orbit and launch association are the only evidence available; the COSPAR id's launch field is the fastest way to tie one back to its flight.

MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.
COMSuperView (Gaojing, 高景) — sub-metre commercial optical imaging operated by China Siwei / SpaceView. Marketed internationally against Maxar and Airbus imagery.

DUALBeiDou is China's global navigation system and the strategic point of the whole programme: ending dependence on GPS, a system the US can degrade regionally at will. BDS-3 was declared complete in July 2020 with a 30-satellite core — 24 in MEO at ~21,500 km, 3 in inclined geosynchronous orbit (IGSO) and 3 in GEO. The IGSO and GEO components are what distinguish BeiDou's architecture from GPS: they concentrate signal strength and availability over China and the Asia-Pacific, including in urban canyons and at high latitudes where a pure MEO constellation thins out. BeiDou also carries a short-message two-way service GPS has no equivalent of. Earlier BDS-2 spacecraft remain in the catalogue, some operational, some drifting as spares or retired; replenishment BDS-3 launches have continued past the 2020 completion date, so the catalogue count runs well above the 30-satellite nominal constellation.

COMJilin-1, operated by Chang Guang Satellite Technology — a spin-out of the CAS Changchun Institute and China's largest commercial imaging constellation, with video as well as still capability. Chang Guang has stated a 300-satellite goal. Commercially sold imagery with a declared revisit rate fine enough to be operationally useful, which is why the constellation appears in military-utility assessments despite its private ownership.

DUALGaofen (高分, 'high resolution') is the space segment of CHEOS, the China High-resolution Earth Observation System, managed by SASTIND. The series splits cleanly at number 8: Gaofen-1 to -7 are genuinely civil, documented in eoPortal and WMO OSCAR with published instruments and open data, serving agriculture, disaster response and mapping. Gaofen-8 and above have had no technical detail released at all, which is itself the evidence analysts rely on — SpaceNews notes the information blackout above GF-7, and the USCC's counterspace assessment describes PRC space assets as assigned military or dual-use and mobilisable in a crisis. The civil branding is real; so is the military customer behind the higher numbers.

DUALBeiDou is China's global navigation system and the strategic point of the whole programme: ending dependence on GPS, a system the US can degrade regionally at will. BDS-3 was declared complete in July 2020 with a 30-satellite core — 24 in MEO at ~21,500 km, 3 in inclined geosynchronous orbit (IGSO) and 3 in GEO. The IGSO and GEO components are what distinguish BeiDou's architecture from GPS: they concentrate signal strength and availability over China and the Asia-Pacific, including in urban canyons and at high latitudes where a pure MEO constellation thins out. BeiDou also carries a short-message two-way service GPS has no equivalent of. Earlier BDS-2 spacecraft remain in the catalogue, some operational, some drifting as spares or retired; replenishment BDS-3 launches have continued past the 2020 completion date, so the catalogue count runs well above the 30-satellite nominal constellation.
CIVThe Tiangong space station and its elements — Tianhe core module, the Wentian and Mengtian laboratory modules, and the Tianzhou cargo freighters that resupply them.

CIVFengyun (风云, 'wind and cloud') — China's operational meteorological satellites, in two families: odd numbers in sun-synchronous polar orbit, even numbers in geostationary. Fengyun data is distributed internationally through the WMO and is a genuine public good. The series also carries the programme's worst moment: the destruction of Fengyun-1C in the January 2007 ASAT test.

COMCentiSpace — a commercial LEO navigation-augmentation constellation from Beijing Future Navigation. LEO augmentation sharpens GNSS convergence time and accuracy, and a LEO signal is far harder to jam than a MEO one because it arrives much stronger.

MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

The civil branding is real; so is the military customer behind the higher numbers.

DUALGaofen (高分, 'high resolution') is the space segment of CHEOS, the China High-resolution Earth Observation System, managed by SASTIND. The series splits cleanly at number 8: Gaofen-1 to -7 are genuinely civil, documented in eoPortal and WMO OSCAR with published instruments and open data, serving agriculture, disaster response and mapping. Gaofen-8 and above have had no technical detail released at all, which is itself the evidence analysts rely on — SpaceNews notes the information blackout above GF-7, and the USCC's counterspace assessment describes PRC space assets as assigned military or dual-use and mobilisable in a crisis. The civil branding is real; so is the military customer behind the higher numbers.

MILYaogan (遥感, 'remote sensing') is the PLA's principal imaging-reconnaissance line, announced only as scientific experiments and land survey. Western analysis has read the series by orbit since its 2006 start: SSO sun-synchronous singles are optical or SAR imagers of the JB-series, while the triplet clusters at ~63.4° in formation are naval electronic-intelligence packages — the direct analogue of the US NOSS ocean-surveillance constellation, locating ships by time-difference-of-arrival across the three spacecraft. Yaogan is the largest single named PRC payload family in the catalogue.

DUALBeiDou is China's global navigation system and the strategic point of the whole programme: ending dependence on GPS, a system the US can degrade regionally at will. BDS-3 was declared complete in July 2020 with a 30-satellite core — 24 in MEO at ~21,500 km, 3 in inclined geosynchronous orbit (IGSO) and 3 in GEO. The IGSO and GEO components are what distinguish BeiDou's architecture from GPS: they concentrate signal strength and availability over China and the Asia-Pacific, including in urban canyons and at high latitudes where a pure MEO constellation thins out. BeiDou also carries a short-message two-way service GPS has no equivalent of. Earlier BDS-2 spacecraft remain in the catalogue, some operational, some drifting as spares or retired; replenishment BDS-3 launches have continued past the 2020 completion date, so the catalogue count runs well above the 30-satellite nominal constellation.

MILTongxin Jishu Shiyan (通信技术试验卫星, 'communications technology experiment satellite') — a cover designation, not a mission description. CASC announces each one with near-identical boilerplate about communications, broadcasting and data-transmission technology verification, and releases nothing further. The analyst consensus, led by Jonathan McDowell's GCAT and Gunter's Space Page, is that TJS bundles at least three distinct programmes: a Qianshao-3 SIGINT class, a Huoyan-1 missile early-warning class, and an unclassified remainder. Attribution to a class is inferred from orbit, launch vehicle and cadence, never confirmed — Gunter's notes that satellites grouped together on those grounds may turn out to have different missions.

MILTianping (天平, 'balance') — radar calibration targets. Spheres and simple bodies of precisely known radar cross-section, used to calibrate ground radars and refine atmospheric-drag models. Unglamorous and quietly important: the accuracy of a space surveillance network is set by what it has to calibrate against.
No public technical detail has been released for this satellite, and no series attribution is established in the open sources. Orbit, launch date and the COSPAR launch id are the available evidence.

DUALBeiDou is China's global navigation system and the strategic point of the whole programme: ending dependence on GPS, a system the US can degrade regionally at will. BDS-3 was declared complete in July 2020 with a 30-satellite core — 24 in MEO at ~21,500 km, 3 in inclined geosynchronous orbit (IGSO) and 3 in GEO. The IGSO and GEO components are what distinguish BeiDou's architecture from GPS: they concentrate signal strength and availability over China and the Asia-Pacific, including in urban canyons and at high latitudes where a pure MEO constellation thins out. BeiDou also carries a short-message two-way service GPS has no equivalent of. Earlier BDS-2 spacecraft remain in the catalogue, some operational, some drifting as spares or retired; replenishment BDS-3 launches have continued past the 2020 completion date, so the catalogue count runs well above the 30-satellite nominal constellation.

DUALGaofen (高分, 'high resolution') is the space segment of CHEOS, the China High-resolution Earth Observation System, managed by SASTIND. The series splits cleanly at number 8: Gaofen-1 to -7 are genuinely civil, documented in eoPortal and WMO OSCAR with published instruments and open data, serving agriculture, disaster response and mapping. Gaofen-8 and above have had no technical detail released at all, which is itself the evidence analysts rely on — SpaceNews notes the information blackout above GF-7, and the USCC's counterspace assessment describes PRC space assets as assigned military or dual-use and mobilisable in a crisis. The civil branding is real; so is the military customer behind the higher numbers.

DUALGaofen (高分, 'high resolution') is the space segment of CHEOS, the China High-resolution Earth Observation System, managed by SASTIND. The series splits cleanly at number 8: Gaofen-1 to -7 are genuinely civil, documented in eoPortal and WMO OSCAR with published instruments and open data, serving agriculture, disaster response and mapping. The civil branding is real; so is the military customer behind the higher numbers.

DUALBeiDou is China's global navigation system and the strategic point of the whole programme: ending dependence on GPS, a system the US can degrade regionally at will. BDS-3 was declared complete in July 2020 with a 30-satellite core — 24 in MEO at ~21,500 km, 3 in inclined geosynchronous orbit (IGSO) and 3 in GEO. The IGSO and GEO components are what distinguish BeiDou's architecture from GPS: they concentrate signal strength and availability over China and the Asia-Pacific, including in urban canyons and at high latitudes where a pure MEO constellation thins out. BeiDou also carries a short-message two-way service GPS has no equivalent of. Earlier BDS-2 spacecraft remain in the catalogue, some operational, some drifting as spares or retired; replenishment BDS-3 launches have continued past the 2020 completion date, so the catalogue count runs well above the 30-satellite nominal constellation.

MILDestroyed on 11 January 2007 by a Chinese SC-19 direct-ascent anti-satellite missile, at about 865 km — the single worst debris-generating event in the history of spaceflight. More than 3,000 catalogued fragments, the majority still in orbit two decades later and expected to remain for centuries. The test is the origin point of modern counterspace policy debate and of the international norm-setting effort against destructive ASAT testing; it is kept in this catalogue although the satellite no longer exists, because the debris field it created is still the defining feature of that altitude band. NAZAR's Debris Tracker carries the fragments and a long-read on the test.

CIVFengyun (风云, 'wind and cloud') — China's operational meteorological satellites, in two families: odd numbers in sun-synchronous polar orbit, even numbers in geostationary. Fengyun data is distributed internationally through the WMO and is a genuine public good. The series also carries the programme's worst moment: the destruction of Fengyun-1C in the January 2007 ASAT test.

DUALShijian (实践, 'practice') is China's long-running technology-demonstration line, and the label covers everything from benign materials experiments to the most closely watched spacecraft in the catalogue. Several Shijian vehicles have performed documented rendezvous and proximity operations in GEO; commercial trackers (ExoAnalytic, COMSPOC) and ISR University follow them because an inspection capability and a co-orbital counterspace capability are the same hardware pointed at different targets.
